title: AI and Learning
text:
One of the biggest fears about artificial intelligence in education is the loss of human intelligence. The specific concern is that using AI will replace the need to learn, and with it the human ability to learn. The right tools in the right hands can do a lot of good, and there is also real potential for harm and waste.
I’m an enthusiastic proponent of experts using AI to build tools that deepen student engagement and learning. For me, the sweet spot is using AI to develop an advanced, specialized tool that enhances learning, rather than using it to do the work of learning on our behalf.
Ian Howell, Theodora Nestorova, and I talked about AI and teaching on the VocalFri Podcast in April 2026.






 Dashboard


 Lesson debrief and reflection


 Practice plan and log


I built the portal for my own voice students, and I now use it with all of my private students. After each lesson it transcribes what happened and summarizes what we worked on and how the student responded. It writes an individual practice plan, and before the next lesson it prepares a brief for me from the student’s past lessons, reflections, and repertoire. Students see their progress, reflections, and plans on their own page. In 2026 the portal won the Pan American Vocology Association’s Best Microworkshop/ToolTalk award.
The portal is written in Python and uses the Claude API from Anthropic, with Supabase for the database and logins. The AI’s instructions are based on my teaching framework, including the co-investigation model, motor learning phases, an exercise taxonomy, and safety guidelines. The demo uses sample student data, so you can look around without an account.
Try the demo Visit the studio portal




The archive holds the studies our graduate vocal pedagogy students have completed at Boston Conservatory at Berklee, 33 so far, from 2022 to 2026, across 17 topics. It gives any student beginning thesis research in vocal pedagogy, at Boston Conservatory or elsewhere, a clear starting point and models to learn from. Readers can search the catalog, follow a topic across cohorts, and explore the data in interactive figures. I built the archive with Claude, Anthropic’s AI model, and maintain it the same way.
Go to the research archive





In my History of Vocal Pedagogy seminar, each graduate student researches a pedagogue and adds events to a shared class timeline. With Claude, I turned the class’s contributions into an interactive timeline of 36 pedagogues, from Pier Francesco Tosi in the 1600s to the present, shown alongside major publications, musical periods, and world events. Readers can zoom in and turn each layer on or off, which makes it easier to see who was teaching at the same time and what was happening around them. Every student who contributed worked from widely available sources and gave consent for their contributions to be shared.
Open the full timeline



Of course, a clear understanding of the settings for data security and privacy is incredibly important, and so is informed consent.
Before a student uses the studio portal, they read and accept a consent form that explains what the portal does, how their information is stored and used, and what their rights are. Using the portal is voluntary and has no effect on a student’s standing in my studio, and students who would rather not use it can work out another arrangement with me. They can withdraw their consent or ask me to delete their data at any time. Studio data are never used for research without a separate consent process approved by Berklee’s institutional review board.
In the portal, lesson audio is transcribed on my own computer and is never sent to an outside transcription service. Before a transcript goes to Claude, the student’s name is replaced with an identifier, and I have opted out of Anthropic using my data to train its models. Lesson records are kept in a protected database where each student can see only their own. I review everything the AI writes before a student sees it.
In the research archive, all data are confidentialized under Berklee’s institutional review board, and participants are identified only by number.



I think teachers should be involved in building the AI tools they will use. I’m open to consulting and advisory work with companies building learning technology and with schools rethinking how teachers are trained.
Get in touch

title: About
text:
I’m a mezzo-soprano, voice teacher, scholar, and program leader. At Boston Conservatory at Berklee, where I’m Assistant Professor of Voice and Vocal Pedagogy, I lead the graduate vocal pedagogy area and supervise graduate students’ research.



   

I trained as a singer at San Diego State University, where I studied vocal performance, and I started teaching voice privately in 2012. While I was still a student, I co-founded the Folklore Guild, a choir that sang music from video games and films. I also spent three years as Director of Development and Education for Bach Collegium San Diego, a professional early music ensemble. I helped double its annual budget, and grants from the National Endowment for the Arts and the City of San Diego paid for open rehearsals and lectures for students in Title I schools.




I came to Boston for a master’s degree in vocal pedagogy at New England Conservatory and stayed on after graduating, as Assistant Vocal Pedagogy Director on the faculty and as manager of the Voice and Sound Analysis Lab. In 2019 I joined the faculty of the Acoustic Vocal Pedagogy Workshop, now run by the Embodied Music Lab. When the pandemic moved lessons online, Ian Howell and I ran SoundJack Bootcamp to help musicians rehearse together over the internet, and we published a comparison of audio quality on the main video-call platforms. During the same years I worked as a research assistant at the Massachusetts General Hospital (MGH) Voice Center on a study of ambulatory voice monitoring.



 Photo: Simon Simard for Berklee
Boston Conservatory hired me in 2022 to lead the research side of its graduate degrees in voice teaching and singing. My job was to help students learn to read research closely, design studies of their own, and publish what they find. Since then we have built a voice science lab and a thesis sequence in quantitative and mixed methods, with institutional review board (IRB) review for every study. I have also strengthened the conservatory’s existing partnership with the MGH Voice Center, which gives incoming voice students a screening and follow-up care. Our students’ theses are collected in a public research archive.
In 2024 I took on leadership of the whole area, including the MM in Vocal Pedagogy and the MFA in Musical Theater Vocal Pedagogy. Since 2022 our alumni have given 35 conference presentations, 19 of them at the Voice Foundation’s annual symposium, and graduates now teach at Oberlin, Brown, Catholic University of America, Oklahoma State, and UMass Amherst. I also direct the Vocal Pedagogy Professional Workshop, a summer program for working voice teachers, and Vocal Academy, where adult singers study with our graduate students. In 2023 the National Association of Teachers of Singing (NATS) gave me its Voice Pedagogy Award.



 Photo: Simon Simard for Berklee
I call my approach scientific method informed voice teaching. In a lesson I listen and watch, the student tells me what they feel, and we decide together what to try next. We keep what is observable, measurable, and repeatable, and over time students learn to run these experiments without me. I talked about this approach on the VocalFri Podcast in 2025.


I supervise graduate research the same way. Students start from something they have noticed in their own teaching or singing and turn it into a question they can test.




In 2024 I started building the AI Supported Voice Studio Portal for my private students. After each lesson it produces a debrief and a practice plan, and between lessons students use it to log their practice and reflect on how it went. In 2026 it won the Pan American Vocology Association’s Best Microworkshop/ToolTalk award. More about my work with AI.
I want good voice pedagogy training to be available to teachers who cannot move to a conservatory city or pay conservatory tuition, and most of what I build now is meant for them.



I present regularly at the Voice Foundation Symposium, the Pan American Vocology Association, and the National Association of Teachers of Singing, usually with the graduate students whose research I supervise. Recent work includes:

title: Teaching
text:
Photo: Simon Simard for Berklee
I lead two graduate degrees at Boston Conservatory at Berklee. The MM in Vocal Pedagogy is a 36-credit degree for singers who want to learn the science and craft of voice teaching, with pedagogy training in classical, musical theater, and contemporary styles. The MFA in Musical Theater Vocal Pedagogy is a 60-credit terminal degree for teachers who specialize in musical theater, and it includes an original thesis.
Program details and how to apply




Incoming voice students receive a voice screening at the MGH Voice Center at Massachusetts General Hospital, and those with findings receive physician follow-up. The partnership with MGH predates my time here, and I have worked to strengthen it.



 Photo: Simon Simard for Berklee
The whole cohort meets each week in the Vocal Pedagogy Colloquium, which I created and co-teach with Emily Siar. Students bring video of their own teaching for the group to discuss, teach live in front of their classmates, and hear from guest teachers. Both degrees now require it.



At the end of the spring, students teach a fifteen-minute lesson and then talk through their choices with a panel of two faculty members. Emily Siar and I developed the rubric for this exam, and we talked about it on the Berklee VoiceCast in July 2026.




MFA students spend three semesters on an original thesis, from the first question through data collection, analysis, and defense. They work in our voice science lab, which has acoustic analysis in Praat, heart rate and respiration monitoring, and Python data pipelines, and every study goes through institutional review board (IRB) review. Since 2022, alumni of the program have given 35 conference presentations, including 19 at the Voice Foundation, 7 at the Pan American Vocology Association, and 6 at the National Association of Teachers of Singing (NATS). Their theses are collected in a public research archive.



Graduates teach at Oberlin Conservatory, Catholic University of America, Oklahoma State University, UMass Amherst, Brown University, and other schools. The program’s website has profiles of our alumni and current students.





 Photo: Simon Simard for Berklee
Each summer I direct the Vocal Pedagogy Professional Workshop (VPPW), four days for collegiate and private voice teachers and vocal and choral music educators working in classical, musical theater, and contemporary styles. You can join in person at Boston Conservatory or online. The program mixes lectures and master classes with mentored teaching in small afternoon cohorts. No audition is required.
Skill up your studio teaching at VPPW
Since 2019 I have also been on the faculty of the Acoustic Vocal Pedagogy Workshop, run by the Embodied Music Lab.



I also direct Vocal Academy, which pairs adult singers with the graduate students in our MM and MFA programs. Each semester includes ten one-hour private lessons in classical, musical theater, or contemporary singing, scheduled around your week. It is open to anyone 18 or older, with no audition.
Study with our graduate student teachers



 Photo: Simon Simard for Berklee
I teach voice lessons and coach voice teachers privately, in person in the Boston area or online.
Visit the studio site
